title: Careers & Certifications
summary: The main cybersecurity roles, how people get into them, and which certifications are worth your time.

lessons.title: Cybersecurity career paths

concept.text:
Cybersecurity is not one job. It is a family of roles that broadly split into **blue team** (defending: monitoring, responding, hardening), **red team** (attacking with permission to find weaknesses) and **governance, risk and compliance** (GRC: policy, audits and risk).

Most people do not start in security. They start in IT support, networking, system administration or software development, and move across once they understand how systems work. You cannot protect what you do not understand.
concept.analogy: Security roles are like the jobs in a hospital. There are emergency responders (incident response), specialists who diagnose (analysts), people who stress-test the system (penetration testers) and administrators who make sure rules are followed (GRC). Different temperaments suit different roles.

steps.title: Build the foundations
steps.text: Learn networking (the Networking tab), operating systems (Linux and Windows), and some scripting in Python or Bash. These underpin every role.

steps.title: Get hands-on
steps.text: Build a home lab. Practise on legal platforms such as TryHackMe, Hack The Box and OverTheWire. Play capture the flag (CTF) competitions. Employers hire evidence of practical skill.

steps.title: Show your work
steps.text: Write up what you built and learned on a blog or GitHub: a lab build, a CTF solution, a detection rule. A portfolio distinguishes you from other applicants with the same certificate.

steps.title: Take a realistic first job
steps.text: Help desk, junior system administrator and SOC tier 1 are the common entry points. Expect to spend a year or two there, learning how real environments work.

questions.q: Which role spends its day triaging and investigating alerts from a SIEM?
questions.explain: SOC analysts are the front line of detection and response.

questions.q: What does a red team do?
options: Simulates real attackers, with authorisation, to test defences
questions.explain: Red teams attack with permission. Blue teams defend.

questions.q: What is the most common route into a first security job?
options: Through IT support, networking or administration
By hacking a company without permission
questions.explain: Operational IT experience teaches how systems really work. Unauthorised hacking is a crime.

questions.q: Which activity best demonstrates practical skill to an employer?
options: A documented home lab and CTF write-ups
questions.explain: Documented, hands-on work is evidence that you can do the job.

challenge.prompt: Write a six-month plan for someone working on an IT help desk who wants to become a SOC analyst. Include what to learn, what to build and what to show.
challenge.hint: Combine one certification, one lab project, regular practice and something public.
challenge.solution:
**Months 1-2**: study networking fundamentals and begin Security+. Build a home lab with a firewall and two or three VMs.

**Months 3-4**: sit Security+. Install a free SIEM such as Wazuh or the Elastic stack in the lab, send it logs, and write a few detection rules. Work through blue-team learning paths on TryHackMe.

**Month 5**: simulate attacks in the lab (a port scan, a brute-force login) and document how you detected each one, mapped to MITRE ATT&CK.

**Month 6**: publish the write-ups on GitHub or a blog, ask to shadow your employer's security team, and apply for SOC tier 1 roles. Then start CySA+.

takeaways: Security has blue team, red team and GRC paths. Choose by interest and temperament.
Most people enter through IT support, networking or administration.
Hands-on labs and a public portfolio matter as much as certificates.

lessons.title: Certifications: Security+, CySA+ and beyond

concept.text:
Certifications are exams that show employers you have a defined level of knowledge. In cybersecurity they matter more than in most fields: many job adverts and government contracts name them as requirements.

They are a signal, not a substitute for skill. The best approach is to pick the certification that matches the next job you want, study it alongside hands-on practice, and avoid collecting certificates for their own sake.
concept.analogy: A certification is a driving licence. It proves you passed a standard test and lets you apply for the job. It does not make you a good driver. Hours behind the wheel do that.

visual.caption: A sensible progression. Most certifications must be renewed about every three years.
rows: A first IT job on a help desk
Network and support roles, and the base for security
The baseline security certification, widely required
Senior and leadership roles. Requires five years of experience.

steps.title: Start with Security+
steps.text: It covers threats, architecture, operations, identity, cryptography and risk at a foundation level. It is vendor-neutral and the most commonly requested entry-level security certification. Much of this tab maps to its objectives.

steps.title: Choose a direction
steps.text: For defence, take **CySA+** next. For offence, take **PenTest+** and then the hands-on **OSCP**. For cloud, add a provider's security certification.

steps.title: Study effectively
steps.text: Download the official exam objectives and use them as a checklist. Combine a course or book with labs and timed practice exams. Book the exam date early: a deadline focuses study.

steps.title: Plan for the long term
steps.text: **CISSP** is the standard for senior roles, but needs five years of paid experience. Keep certifications current with continuing education credits.

interactive.prompt: Arrange this common blue-team certification path from first to last.

challenge.prompt: Two people ask your advice. Sam is a network technician with three years of experience who wants to move into a SOC. Alex is a software developer who wants to become a penetration tester. Recommend the next two certifications for each, with reasons.
challenge.hint: Do not send experienced people back to the very beginning. Match the certificate to the target role.
challenge.solution:
**Sam (network technician to SOC)**: skip A+ and probably Network+, because three years of networking already covers them. Take **Security+** for the security baseline, then **CySA+**, which focuses on detection, log analysis and incident response: exactly what SOC work involves.

**Alex (developer to penetration tester)**: take **Security+** for broad fundamentals if security is new, then **PenTest+**, or go straight to studying for **OSCP** if comfortable in labs. A developer's understanding of code is a real advantage for web application testing, so plenty of practice on Hack The Box and with the OWASP Top 10 is as important as the certificates.

takeaways: Security+ is the baseline. CySA+ leads to blue team work, PenTest+ and OSCP to red team work.
CISSP is for experienced professionals and requires five years in the field.
Match the certification to your next role, and always pair study with hands-on practice.
